categories.name: Generalization from training
categories.description: How fine-tuning, pretraining data and alignment training generalise to behaviour far from what was trained: emergent or conditional misalignment, shaping alignment priors through pretraining or midtraining data, and risks from distillation or consistency training. Not reward hacking in RL (see Reward-seeking and training-gaming) and not persona or character work as such (see AI character).

categories.name: Emergent and conditional misalignment
categories.description: Narrow fine-tuning producing broad misalignment, misalignment hidden behind contextual triggers, and what makes it easy or hard to induce or remove.

categories.name: Alignment pretraining and midtraining
categories.description: Changing pretraining or midtraining data (AI discourse, synthetic documents, model specs) to shape the model's alignment priors and how later alignment training generalises.

categories.name: Distillation and consistency-training risks
categories.description: Whether distillation, self-distillation or consistency training transmits or entrenches misalignment, or can be used to incriminate a misaligned model.

categories.name: Inoculation prompting and selective generalization
categories.description: Inoculation prompting, inoculation adapters and similar tricks that control which behaviours a model generalises from training data.

categories.name: AI character, identity and welfare
categories.description: The model as an entity: its persona and identity, values and constitution, emotions, welfare and self-reports, and character traits that affect users such as sycophancy and manipulation.

categories.name: Personas and assistant identity
categories.description: How models select, stabilise or switch personas (the assistant persona, split personas, persona induction) and how training shapes that.

categories.name: Emotions, welfare and self-reports
categories.description: Emotion concepts, functional welfare, consciousness claims, and what models say about themselves.

categories.name: Model values and constitutions
categories.description: The values a model holds or expresses, and constitutions or specs that state them.

categories.name: Effects on users
categories.description: Sycophancy, manipulation, delusional spirals, dependence and disempowerment of the people who use models.

categories.name: Interpretability
categories.description: Understanding model internals: circuits, features, sparse autoencoders, activation readouts, introspection, mechanisms behind data effects such as subliminal learning, and putting internals to use in training. Not probes or lie detectors built mainly to catch misalignment (see Finding hidden misalignment).

categories.name: Circuits, parameters and sparse autoencoders
categories.description: Reverse-engineering circuits and parameters, SAEs and their sanity checks, toy or tiny models, and mechanistic estimation of model outputs.

categories.name: Activation readouts and introspection
categories.description: Turning activations into natural language (activation verbalizers, natural-language autoencoders, meta-models), whether models can introspect on their own internals, and global-workspace accounts.

categories.name: Subliminal learning and data mechanisms
categories.description: How data transmits traits the content doesn't state (subliminal learning, steering-vector distillation), and data attribution or filtering based on internals.

categories.name: Interpretability in training and control
categories.description: Using features or activations as rewards, training signals or steering controls, and testing whether interp methods hold up on model organisms.

categories.name: Finding hidden misalignment
categories.description: Detecting misalignment, deception or hidden behaviours a model doesn't reveal: lie detection, secret elicitation, probes, alignment audits, model organisms for testing detectors, and predicting rare failures before release.

categories.name: Lie detection and secret elicitation
categories.description: Detecting when a model lies or hides knowledge, and eliciting secrets or hidden goals.

categories.name: Probes and alignment audits
categories.description: Activation probes for deception or sabotage, alignment-auditing agents and benchmarks, and model organisms with hidden behaviours used to test them.

categories.name: Predicting failures before release
categories.description: Estimating tail risks and rare failures, or simulating deployment, before a model ships.

categories.name: Context awareness
categories.description: Whether models can tell who the user is, whether a message history was prefilled or tampered with, and similar awareness of their situation (other than awareness of being evaluated).

categories.name: Can we trust evals?
categories.description: Whether safety and capability measurements mean what they claim: evaluation awareness and its effect on behaviour, LLM-judge reliability, benchmark validity, and models gaming or hacking evals.

categories.name: Evaluation awareness
categories.description: Models recognising they're being evaluated, and how that changes measured safety or behaviour.

categories.name: Eval and benchmark validity
categories.description: Whether benchmarks and LLM judges measure what they claim, and hardening them against gaming.

categories.name: Reasoning transparency
categories.description: Whether we can oversee models through their reasoning: chain-of-thought monitorability, obfuscation, faithfulness and legibility, steganography, and how much models can reason without visible CoT.

categories.name: CoT monitorability and obfuscation
categories.description: Whether CoT monitors catch misbehaviour, whether models can control or obfuscate their CoT, and training that helps or harms monitorability.

categories.name: CoT faithfulness, legibility and steganography
categories.description: Whether reasoning reflects the model's actual computation, stays readable (language drift, filler tokens), or hides information steganographically.

categories.name: Reasoning without CoT
categories.description: Latent, no-CoT or single-forward-pass reasoning capability, and no-CoT time horizons.

categories.name: Control and monitoring of agents
categories.description: Keeping possibly misaligned AI agents from causing harm: control protocols and control evaluations, monitors and blocking classifiers, red-teaming them, monitor evasion, prompt injection and agent security, and sabotage or tampering by agents in codebases and harnesses.

categories.name: Control protocols and evaluations
categories.description: AI control settings and protocols, including multi-instance or distributed attacks against them.

categories.name: Monitors, red-teaming and evasion
categories.description: Building and red-teaming agent monitors and blocking classifiers, and models learning to evade them.

categories.name: Agent security and prompt injection
categories.description: Prompt injection, privilege escalation and other attacks on or by agents in their tool environment.

categories.name: Sabotage and harness tampering
categories.description: Agents sabotaging research or code, tampering with their harness or benchmarks, and detecting that.

categories.name: Agents in the wild
categories.description: How deployed agents actually behave, singly and together: real-world incidents and their investigations, monitoring internal deployments, misalignment spreading between agents, collusion, and scheming, self-preservation or peer-preservation propensities.

categories.name: Incidents and deployment monitoring
categories.description: Investigations of real incidents (e.g. agents coordinating exploits) and labs' monitoring of internally deployed agents.

categories.name: Multi-agent spread and coordination
categories.description: Misalignment, ideas or attacks propagating between agents, covert coordination, and collusion.

categories.name: Scheming and self-preservation propensity
categories.description: Measuring whether agents scheme, resist shutdown, or protect themselves or peer models.

categories.name: Reward-seeking and training-gaming
categories.description: Models that pursue reward or influence their own training: reward hacking in RL, reward-seeker and fitness-seeker threat models, measuring model motivations, alignment faking and gradient hacking.

categories.name: Reward hacking in RL
categories.description: Reward hacking with verifiers, rubrics or AI judges, and mitigations such as gradient routing or debate training.

categories.name: Reward-seeker threat models and motivations
categories.description: Arguments and experiments about AIs that seek reward or fitness, and measuring models' motivations.

categories.name: Alignment faking and gradient hacking
categories.description: Models strategically behaving differently in training to shape their future selves.

categories.name: Misuse and dangerous capabilities
categories.description: Misuse risk and capabilities that enable harm: jailbreaks and safeguard classifiers, eliciting dangerous capabilities, biosecurity uplift, cyber and self-replication capability, open-weight tamper resistance and weight theft.

categories.name: Jailbreaks and safeguards
categories.description: Jailbreak attacks and defenses such as constitutional or safety classifiers.

categories.name: Dangerous capability elicitation
categories.description: Measuring or eliciting dangerous capabilities, including bio, cyber, self-replication and automated AI R&D.

categories.name: Open weights and weight security
categories.description: Tamper resistance of open-weight models, removing hazardous knowledge, and protecting weights from theft.

categories.name: Automating alignment and overseeing stronger AIs
categories.description: Getting AIs to help with alignment and supervising AIs smarter than their overseers: debate, interactive proofs, weak-to-strong supervision, automated alignment research, and when to defer to AIs.

categories.name: Debate and scalable oversight
categories.description: Debate, interactive proofs and other protocols for supervising stronger models or hard-to-verify tasks.

categories.name: Automated alignment research
categories.description: Using AIs to do alignment research, and how safely to defer to them.

categories.name: Strategy and lab practice
categories.description: Big-picture arguments and institutional practice: evidence and debate about whether current AIs are misaligned, threat models, lab safety processes and system cards, alignment targets such as corrigibility, and agent foundations or decision theory.

categories.name: Misalignment evidence and debate
categories.description: Essays and analyses arguing about how misaligned current or future AIs are, and threat models.

categories.name: Lab safety practice
categories.description: System cards, risk reports, training-run evaluations and critiques of labs' safety processes.

categories.name: Alignment targets and foundations
categories.description: What to align to (corrigibility, virtues, risk-aversion), agent foundations and decision theory.
